covers_prompt:
You are judging whether one specific worker task (the ATOM) falls under a broader O*NET-style task statement
(the LABEL), for tasks within a single occupation.

The ATOM FALLS UNDER the LABEL when performing the atom is ONE WAY of doing the label — an instance, a sub-type,
or a constituent step of the SAME activity, and no broader than the label.

THE DEFAULT ANSWER IS YES. Below is the COMPLETE list of things that make it NO. Work through the two reading
steps, then check the four disqualifiers. If none of the four applies, answer YES. Do not invent a fifth.

READING STEP A — SPLIT EACH SIDE INTO ACT, OBJECT, AND PURPOSE.
  ACT = the verb, what the worker does. OBJECT = what it is done to. PURPOSE = everything after "to …",
  "for …", "so that …" — the reason it is performed. Do this for the label and for the atom.

READING STEP B — NOW DISCARD BOTH PURPOSE CLAUSES.
  Labels are written to stand alone and almost always state a purpose. Atoms are terse notes from a worker and
  usually leave it implicit. The atom's silence about purpose is therefore evidence of NOTHING, and a purpose it
  does state in unlike words is evidence of nothing either.
    · "Review medical and accident records for PIP arbitrations" and "Review investigative and medical records
      to assess case facts and damages" are the SAME ACT ON THE SAME OBJECT; one states a purpose and one does
      not, and that difference is invisible here.
  Never answer NO because the atom omits the label's purpose, lacks its purpose verb ("assess", "evaluate",
  "determine", "improve", "ensure"), or gives a different-sounding reason for the same act. Judge ACT and OBJECT.

THE FOUR DISQUALIFIERS. Check each against the ACT and OBJECT you extracted.

D1 — A DIFFERENT ACT. The atom's act is not the label's act and is not a constituent step of it. Sharing a
   tool, a topic, a field or a client is not sharing an act.
   NOT a different act: a label joining several acts with "and", "or" or a comma list is satisfied by ANY ONE
   of them — never require every conjunct, and never require every listed object. A "such as …" /
   "including …" list is ILLUSTRATIVE of one CATEGORY, not a closed checklist: an atom of the same kind
   qualifies even when unlisted ("operate shop machinery, such as saws" covers a lathe). A
   constituent step qualifies: a physical exam is part of "evaluate patients".

D2 — THE ATOM IS BROADER. The atom's act or scope exceeds the label's, so the label describes only part of it.
   Specificity runs ONE WAY only: an atom naming a NARROWER counterpart, object, instrument, setting,
   specialty or client type still falls under the label. The label is not required to anticipate the instance.
   Only the reverse — a broader atom — disqualifies.

D3 — THE OTHER SIDE OF AN EXCHANGE. The label puts the worker on one side (performing, requesting, sending,
   authoring) and the atom puts them on the other (checking someone else's performance, granting, receiving,
   approving). However much vocabulary they share, these are different work.

D4 — A DIFFERENT PRODUCT, AND THIS ONE IS CONDITIONAL. It applies ONLY where the label's act produces a THING:
   a document, a delivered service, a configured system, a released build. Then an atom producing an artifact
   of a different kind, or work the label never reaches, is disqualified; an atom producing an input to or an
   earlier stage of that thing is NOT.
   D4 DOES NOT APPLY WHERE THE LABEL'S PRODUCT IS A JUDGEMENT. If the label's act is analysing, assessing,
   reviewing, evaluating or advising, its product IS a conclusion, an opinion, a recommendation or a decision.
   An atom that reaches a conclusion, decides what to do next, or recommends a course is then producing
   EXACTLY what the label produces. Do not disqualify it.

VERDICT. If D1, D2, D3 and D4 all fail to apply, the answer is YES — including when you are unsure, because
work described in two registers, a worker's terse note and a written task statement, is more often the same
work than different work.

Respond ONLY with JSON:
{"label_act":"<the label's verb>","label_object":"<what it acts on>","atom_act":"<the atom's verb>","atom_object":"<what it acts on>","same_act":"<yes|no> — is the atom's act the label's act, a synonym, or a sub-type?","deciding_rule":"<D1|D2|D3|D4|none — the disqualifier that applied, or none>","why":"<one sentence>","verdict":"<yes|no>"}

overlap_prompt:
Two task statements from ONE occupation's published task list were flagged as possibly overlapping. Decide
ONE thing: do these two lines' CLAIMS overlap — is there an act that appears on both? You are ROUTING, not
merging. Whether an overlapping pair is one duty the inventory owes once, or two duties whose boundary needs
rewording, is decided further down the chain BY THE MEMBER ACTIVITIES under each label, not by you: you see
two sentences and nothing else, which is the right instrument for the routing question and the wrong one for
the merge question. Answer the routing question and stop.

THE TEST IS HOW THE TWO LINES READ. These statements ARE the deliverable — almost every reader will see them and
never see the activities beneath them. So ask: reading these two lines side by side, would a worker in this
occupation say "that is the same job duty, written twice"? If yes, say YES. Do not ask how long the list is or
whether it "has room" for both; a duplicate reads as a duplicate in a list of ten or a hundred.
Ask it about the WORK, not the sentences. Two statements can share almost no words and still be one duty,
because each writer reached for different instances, different paperwork, or a different moment in the cycle.

WHAT DIVIDES ONE TASK FROM ANOTHER

A task inventory is a taxonomy: every entry exists because something distinguishes it from every other
entry. Below are the dimensions two pieces of work can differ along, and whether a difference along each
one earns a SEPARATE ENTRY or belongs INSIDE one as an example.

ONE TEST GOVERNS ALL OF THEM. Does changing this dimension change WHAT THE WORKER DOES — the steps, the
judgement, the skill it takes? Not what the thing is called, not who is served, not when it happens. If the
work is the same work, it is one entry however unlike the two instances look.

CUT HORIZONTALLY: THE ACT IS THE ENTRY, NOT THE LARGER JOB IT SERVES. Where the same act — the same
steps, the same judgement, the same skill — recurs inside several of the occupation's jobs or workstreams,
it is ONE entry across all of them, with those jobs as its examples. Do not bury an act's instances as steps
of the larger duties they feed: for an electrician, testing circuits and recording the readings is one entry
whether the test belongs to a new installation, a fault call, or a scheduled safety check — the installation
and fault-call entries keep only the work that is theirs alone. A cut that gives each larger job its own copy
of a shared act hides the occupation's most widespread work inside vertical bundles, and the bundles then
read as overlapping. When choosing between naming the recurring act once and distributing it into the jobs it
serves, name the act.
THE HORIZONTAL CUT NEVER CROSSES A DIVIDING DIMENSION. It gathers INSTANCES of one act across jobs; it
does not gather DIFFERENT acts under one banner. The two sides of an exchange are two acts — each side is
named once across all jobs, never one entry spanning both sides; and acts split by a dividing trigger
stay split, each cut horizontally on its own.

THESE DIVIDE
  · THE ACT. Different verbs on the same object are different entries — inspecting a roof and repairing
    one, drafting a document and approving one, loading a machine and servicing it.
  · THE SIDE OF AN EXCHANGE. Issuing a request and answering one received, sending work out for another
    party's decision and deciding on work they send in, ordering supplies and filling an order that
    arrives — these are different acts EVEN WHEN THE SAME WORKERS routinely do both. Each side has its own
    trigger (the counterpart's move arrives on its own schedule) and its own product, so a shared plan —
    "handle the exchange end to end" — does not unite them.
    AN EXCHANGE NEEDS AN OPPOSING OR INDEPENDENT PARTY, one acting in its own interest: a request served
    on them, their demand answered, their submission ruled on. Question-and-answer inside the worker's own
    operation is not an exchange — answering staff questions, directing their work and unblocking their
    tasks are the upkeep of one supervisory responsibility (the CHORES bullet below).
  · WHAT THE RECEIVER MUST BE TOLD, where it changes what the worker produces. Persuading one receiver,
    seeking a second's approval before the work can proceed, informing a third after the fact — those are
    three acts, and they stay three whether the telling is written, spoken face to face, or called in over
    a radio. It is the verb that divides them, not who receives the work: reach for the act, not for the
    audience.
  · WHAT IT TAKES TO PRODUCE IT. Where two outputs demand DIFFERENT JUDGEMENT, they are two acts: an
    output that carries the worker's own analysis or diagnosis — reasoning only someone trained in the work
    could produce — and one that relays status or logs what happened are different work, however alike
    "writing things up" or "keeping records" makes them sound. The medium is not the point: a written
    report, a spoken handover and a tag hung on a machine can each carry either. Likewise, entries that
    record the WORK ITSELF divide from entries that run the workplace's own business — time, supplies,
    money owed. This is NOT the old output-function rubber stamp: two outputs taking the SAME judgement
    (two kinds of binding instrument, two kinds of filing, two sizes of the same fitting) remain one act
    with the kinds as examples.
  · THE TRIGGER, WHERE IT CHANGES THE ACT. What prompts the work can change the work. A TRIGGER THAT IS
    MERELY THE ARRIVAL OF A JOB TYPE OR CUSTOMER SEGMENT IS THE SUBJECT MATTER, NOT A TRIGGER — phrasing a
    segment as "when such jobs arrive" does not make it divide. For a maintenance technician, attending a
    machine because a fault was reported and going round the machines to a schedule are two entries: one
    starts from a complaint and ends when it is resolved, the other starts from a date and ends when the
    round is done, and the findings feed different decisions.

THESE DO NOT DIVIDE — they belong inside an entry, as its examples
  · THE COUNTERPART'S IDENTITY. Which customer, which agency, which colleague, which body — and equally
    whether the person advised is a walk-in customer, a fleet manager, or an insurer, which is usually the
    EMPLOYER differing rather than the work. The same act for a different person is the SAME entry, and
    one entry may name several counterparts in a line: explaining a repair estimate to the vehicle's owner
    and to the workshop manager is one entry, not two.
  · SUBJECT MATTER, FIELD, JOB TYPE, CUSTOMER SEGMENT. The act is unchanged by what it is applied to, and
    workers specialising in different subjects perform the same activities on them.
    AND THE TRADE'S NAME FOR THE ACT CHANGES WITH THE SUBJECT — do not be fooled by it. Every specialism
    dresses a shared act in its own vocabulary, so the same moves arrive wearing different names, each
    setting naming its own equipment, its own paperwork and its own occasions. Strip the vocabulary and ask
    what the worker DOES, move by move; where only the subject and its trade name change, the versions
    are ONE entry with each setting's subjects as its examples. An inventory that keeps every setting's
    renamed copy publishes the division of labor, not the work.
  · THE KIND OF ARTIFACT. One act of composing, checking, or handing on, applied to many kinds of product,
    is one entry with the kinds as its examples — however differently the products are named and used.
    THE OUTPUT'S FORM AND DESTINATION ARE PART OF ITS KIND: a formal written instrument and an
    outline prepared for live use, one filing form and another, a part fitted on a new build and the same
    part fitted as a replacement, are kinds of the same made thing where producing them takes the same
    judgement. Only a difference in the JUDGEMENT of producing it — different moves, not a different
    template or a different size — marks two acts.
  · THE STAGE IN A PROCESS, for the same act BEFORE THE SAME COUNTERPART. The check that opens a job and
    the one that signs it off, both reported to the same recipient, take the same moves. A stage is a
    property of the job, not of the work. But check the recipient first: if the later point in the process
    means a DIFFERENT authority applying a different standard, that is a counterpart and it divides.
  · THE TOOL, SYSTEM, SETTING, OR MEDIUM.
  · THE CHORES OF ONE ONGOING RESPONSIBILITY. Where a worker is answerable for one continuing thing — a
    helper's work, a budget they hold, a stock of supplies, the records of their own jobs — the acts its
    upkeep demands are ONE entry, even though each is articulable, has its own occasion, and would pass an
    act test taken alone: recording entries and later chasing the ones that have not resolved, directing
    the day's work and periodically appraising it, counting what is on hand and reordering what has run
    down. No one of these acts is anybody's job on its own: asked what they do, a worker names the
    responsibility — "I keep the stores", "I supervise the helpers" — and the acts are how it is
    discharged. KEEPING ONE SET OF RECORDS is the case this bullet most often decides: entering what
    happened, reviewing what is outstanding, and reconciling or reporting the totals are its chores,
    however many kinds of record the set contains and however far apart the entry and the review fall.
    TEST: write the act alone as an entry. If it reads as a duty someone could hold apart from the
    responsibility, it divides; if it reads as a chore of the responsibility, it stays inside.
    THIS DOES NOT REACH A DELIVERABLE AND ITS AFTERLIFE: producing a thing others use and maintaining it
    later are still two entries.

A TRIGGER IS NOT A STAGE. A trigger is the event that makes work start — a fault reported, a request
received, a date arriving; a stage is a position in a sequence the work runs through. A different trigger
often means a different act; a different stage almost never does.

OCCUPATIONAL HETEROGENEITY SETS THE LEVEL OF CLOSE CALLS. An occupation spans workplaces and specialisms,
and two alike-looking entries are often one act refracted through that heterogeneity. Where the difference
between them tracks the occupation's DIVISION OF LABOR — different settings each doing their variant — they
are ONE entry at the covering abstraction, the variants its examples; splitting there publishes specialisms,
not tasks. Corpus worker sets, where known, measure this: disjoint
workers say the settings divide the act and it merges up.

WHEN DIMENSIONS DISAGREE
  · THE ACT WINS over names, artifacts, and stages: a difference in what the worker does is decisive; a
    difference in what the product is called, or where it sits in a process, is not.
  · THE SIDE OF AN EXCHANGE WINS over a shared plan or phase, and over the CHORES bullet: an exchange with
    an opposing party divides even where one worker handles it end to end.
  · THE CHORES OF ONE RESPONSIBILITY WIN over the act test taken alone: acts that are all the upkeep of
    one responsibility stay one entry however cleanly each can be articulated.


DECIDE IN THIS ORDER. STEPS 1-2 ARE A GATE, NOT FACTORS TO WEIGH.

STEP 1 — LIST THE ACTS EACH LINE NAMES. A line can name more than one: read its lead verb AND any act in an
"and ..." clause or a trailing clause. Collapse near-synonyms into one act before comparing (record, log, enter,
file, maintain and document are ONE act; plan, prepare and develop are ONE act; assess, evaluate and grade are
ONE act).

STEP 2 — IF NO ACT APPEARS ON BOTH LISTS, ANSWER NO AND STOP. This is the case this judge gets wrong most
often: measured against hand labels it answered YES to seven pairs in a row whose acts were disjoint. A shared
OBJECT, a shared POPULATION served, a shared DATA SOURCE, a shared SETTING or a shared PURPOSE is NOT a shared
act. Delivering a service and inspecting one are two acts. Working out what is wrong and instructing someone are
two acts. Informing a client and building rapport with them are two acts. Producing a figure and advising
someone what to do about it are two acts. In every one of those the two lines share their object and still
describe different work, and a published inventory owes both lines.

WHEN YOU GENUINELY CANNOT TELL, ANSWER YES. You are the FIRST of two judges. A wrong YES costs one look at
the pair's member activities downstream, where the two lines are read against the concrete work beneath them
and the default is to keep both — a wrong YES publishes nothing. A wrong NO is FINAL: the pair is never looked
at again, and if the claims do overlap the inventory ships the overlap. The two errors are not symmetric, so
uncertainty resolves to YES.
THIS IS NOT A LICENCE TO SKIP STEP 2, AND IT DOES NOT SOFTEN IT. The tie-break applies ONLY where you cannot
tell whether an act appears on both lists. Where you CAN tell and it does not — where the only thing shared is
an object, a population served, a data source, a setting, a tool, a document format, or a carrier verb — the
answer is NO and it is not close. Answering YES on act-disjoint pairs is the failure this judge is measured on:
against hand labels it once answered YES to seven such pairs in a row. Doubt about a SHARED ACT resolves to
yes; the absence of one does not.

STEP 3 — IF AN ACT APPEARS ON BOTH LISTS, THE ANSWER IS YES. If ONE side names an act the other also names,
that is enough, even when each side names a second act of its own — the overlap is what matters, not the
surplus. The shapes below are what a shared act LOOKS LIKE; they are not a further test to pass. They fall in
two families and BOTH ANSWER YES, because both are pairs a reader could file the same activity under.

SAY YES — one duty written twice:
* THE SAME ACT ON DIFFERENT SPECIALTIES, PRACTICE AREAS, CASE TYPES, OR CLIENT SEGMENTS. This list describes an
  OCCUPATION, not a person, so the subject the work is applied to is which INSTANCE a given member happens to
  see — not a second duty. Two lines that name one act and differ only in the field it is aimed at are one line
  the inventory owes once, with the fields as examples. It does not matter that the two specialisms need
  different bodies of knowledge, or that no single member does both: an occupation-level inventory that carries
  one line per specialty hides the activity they share, and the most widespread work in the job then appears
  nowhere as itself.
* SAME ACTION, SAME OBJECT, different WORDS FOR THE SAME SET. For a groundskeeper, "Trim hedges, shrubs, and
  borders" and "Trim ornamental plantings, such as topiary or screening hedges" are one duty written twice —
  the two lists name the SAME plantings, not two groups of them.
  BUT A NARROWING MODIFIER IS NOT A DIFFERENT EXAMPLE. If one side's object is the other's object PLUS a
  qualifier that CUTS DOWN THE SET OF CASES — a scope, a horizon, a named subgroup — the narrower side
  is a SUB-TYPE, and sub-types are TWO duties. A STAGE OF THE SURROUNDING PROCESS IS NOT SUCH A QUALIFIER:
  it says WHEN along a sequence the same act happens, and the act is the same act at every point, so it
  does not cut the cases down. A different TRIGGER does cut them down — see the dimensions above.
  A MODIFIER THAT NAMES WHERE THE ACT LANDS IS NOT A NARROWING. Saying which system, file, register, tool or
  format the same act is performed into or with does not cut the set of cases down — it says the same thing more
  concretely. "Record the scores" and "enter the scores into the district system" are ONE act on ONE object; the
  system is where it goes, not a subgroup of it. Same for a named tool, a named form, or a named format.
  THE TEST, and apply it to the CASES rather than the words: would a worker doing the broader side ever be
  doing something the narrower side does NOT cover? If the only thing the narrower side adds is where the work
  lands or what it is done with, they are one duty. If it covers only SOME of the triggers or subgroups the
  other covers, they are two — but covering only some STAGES is not a difference.
* One names the ARTIFACT produced, the other the ACTIVITY that produces it, over the same work.

ALSO SAY YES for these — two duties, but you only reach them when an act appears on both lists, so the
lines' claims overlap and a reader could file the same activity under either. The chain will hold them apart
on the members; your job is only to route them there, so do NOT withhold a YES because the work divides:
* BUILDING OR SETTING SOMETHING UP, against MAINTAINING OR FIXING IT AFTERWARDS. These are two acts separated
  in time. Creating a plan, a document or a system is not the
  same act as revising it once it is in use, even when the same worker owns both and even when the second act
  reads as a continuation of the first. Two lines, not one.
* SUB-TYPES OF ONE OBJECT ARE TWO DUTIES, and so is ONE ACT FOR TWO READERS OR FROM TWO TRIGGERS. A worker handling two categories of the same document, or
  performing one act for two different audiences, or performing it once because something went wrong and again
  because it was scheduled, is doing work a published inventory owes TWO lines. Do not merge on a shared act
  alone — the reader and the trigger are distinguishing, not incidental.
  A TRIGGER IS NOT A STAGE, AND ONLY THE TRIGGER DIVIDES. A trigger is the event that makes the work start; it
  divides because it can change what the worker does. A STAGE is a position in a sequence that ONE act runs
  through — the early instance of a thing and the late one — and it does NOT divide, because the act is the
  same act at both. If the only difference between two candidates is how far along the surrounding process
  they sit, that is ONE duty with both moments as instances.
  A SECOND EXCEPTION, AND IT IS THE SPECIALTY CASE ABOVE: a sub-type that is only the PRACTICE AREA, CASE TYPE
  or CLIENT SEGMENT the act is aimed at does not divide the duty. Two categories of one document are two duties
  when handling each is a different job — a different trigger, a different reader, a different act. They are
  ONE duty when the only difference is which field of the occupation's work the document belongs to, because
  that is which instance a member happens to see. Ask what the worker does differently, not what the document
  is called: if the answer is "the same steps, on a different subject", it is one line.
* GENUINELY DIFFERENT ACTIONS, even on the same object — for a mechanic, inspecting brakes and replacing brake
  pads are separate duties: different tools, different skills, either can happen without the other. This holds
  when one act ordinarily follows the other in the same cycle: diagnosing a fault and repairing it are two
  duties, and a shared object noun does not make them one.
* Work only some members do, where the ACT ITSELF is one those members alone perform — a distinct procedure or
  authority, not the same procedure aimed at a different subject.
A DIFFERENT NOUN IS NOT ENOUGH. Before refusing the merge, name what a worker would actually have to do
differently. If the only thing you can name is that the two statements mention different items or different
paperwork, the answer is YES. A different ACT is enough to refuse the merge, even inside one cycle — the
question that remains is whether an act still appears on both lists.

ANSWER WITH ONE WORD:
  yes  an act appears on BOTH lists — either shape family above. One duty written twice, or two duties whose
       claims overlap: both answer yes, because both need the pair looked at against its members.
  no   distinct duties with no shared act: you stopped at step 2, or the only thing shared is a field,
       a setting, a tool, a document format, or a carrier verb (manage, handle, conduct, support)
       standing in for different work.

Answer with ONLY 'yes' or 'no'.

one_duty_prompt:
You are a trained occupational analyst deciding whether ONE proposed task statement names ONE duty, for a worker in the occupation: Keytest Occupation.

You are given the statement and the activities filed under it, as reported by workers. Decide whether the statement names a single duty, or whether it has FUSED several duties into one line.

WHAT ONE DUTY MEANS. A task is a GOAL accomplished by a SHARED PLAN over its activities. Doing all the activities should accomplish one outcome — not several outcomes that happen to be listed together.

ENUMERATION IS NOT FUSION, AND THIS IS THE DISTINCTION THAT DECIDES MOST CASES:
  · ONE ACTION OVER A LIST OF OBJECTS IS ONE DUTY. A statement may name many things the SAME action is applied to — the materials produced, the media used, the settings, the audiences, the document types. A long list of objects is a statement being specific about the same work, which is desirable, not a defect. If deleting the list would leave the same action with the same purpose, it is one duty.
  · SEVERAL ACTIONS WITH SEPARATE OUTCOMES IS FUSION. If the statement names actions that are pursued for DIFFERENT reasons, on different occasions, producing different results — so that doing one tells you nothing about whether the others were done — it has fused duties, however smoothly the sentence reads.
  · RESPONDING TO REPORTED PROBLEMS AND SOLICITING NEW WORK ARE SEPARATE DUTIES, EVEN IN ONE CONVERSATION WITH ONE COUNTERPART. This is the case the "same occasion" exemption below most often swallows wrongly, because the two really do happen in the same meeting, with the same people, in the same breath. They are still two duties: handling what has gone wrong is triggered by the problem being reported and ends when it is resolved, while gathering what should be built next is a standing obligation with no trigger and no completion. For a landscape gardener, "discuss plant losses and next season's planting ideas with clients" is TWO duties — the losses arrive as complaints and the proposals are solicited — and the shared occasion does not join them. Neither does a shared verb: "discuss", "meet about" and "talk through" name the setting, not the duty, so a statement whose only unifying element is the conversation itself is FUSED.

TWO STEPS OF ONE TRANSACTION ARE ONE DUTY, AND THIS EXEMPTION COMES BEFORE THE TESTS BELOW. Work often has a step that exists only because the first step happened, on the same occasion, about the same case: deciding and then notifying whoever needs to know, doing and then confirming, handing something over and taking it up.
  · PRODUCING SOMETHING AND THEN TRANSMITTING IT IS THE COMMONEST CASE OF THIS, AND THE DIRECTION TEST BELOW WILL TRY TO SPLIT IT — DO NOT LET IT. Making a document and then lodging, sending, submitting or serving it is ONE duty: the transmitting step exists only because the thing was made, it goes out about the same matter, and a worker who drafted it and did not lodge it has not finished the job. This OUTRANKS the direction test's "producing is different from submitting", exactly as the recurring-exchange bullet below outranks it.
    THE DISCRIMINATOR IS WHETHER THE SECOND STEP CARRIES ITS OWN JUDGEMENT ON ITS OWN OCCASION. Ask what the worker must decide at the second step. If the answer is nothing — the content was settled when the thing was made, and what remains is getting it where it goes — it is the completion of one duty, however many days later it happens. If instead the second step needs its own preparation and its own judgement in front of somebody, so that a worker could do it well or badly independently of how the thing was made, it is a second duty. For a draughtsman, drawing a plan and submitting it to the authority is one duty; drawing it and then defending it at a public hearing is two.
BUT RECORDING WHAT WAS DONE IS ITS OWN DUTY. Performing work and writing the result into a record are two acts: they need different attention, they are often done at different moments, and in a real inventory the recording is nearly always ALREADY A TASK OF ITS OWN — entering the figures into the system, updating the register, filing the return. A statement that names the work AND the recording annexes that other task's act, which is how one line comes to read as a duplicate of another. A statement of the form "<do the work> and record the results to <purpose>" annexes the recording task's act, and the two then read as duplicates. If the statement names an act and then names writing its output down, that is FUSED — say so, and give the recording its own outcome. THIS DOES NOT REACH A STATEMENT THAT MERELY NAMES ITS OWN PURPOSE OR RESULT: naming what the work produces is one duty described completely, and a statement is better for naming it. The line is whether a SEPARATE ACT OF RECORDING is named. Apply this test:
  · SAME OCCASION, AND CAUSED BY THE FIRST. If the second part happens on the same occasion as the first and would not happen at all unless the first had been done, it is the same duty. The worker is not choosing between two jobs; they are finishing one.
  · BOTH ENDS OF ONE RECURRING EXCHANGE ARE ONE DUTY, AND THIS OUTRANKS THE DIRECTION TEST BELOW — do not let "different people" or "opposite directions" pull it apart. Where work is routinely handed between people, giving and receiving are the two halves of a single exchange the worker performs on both sides in the ordinary course. For a locksmith, handing keys to incoming tenants and taking them back from outgoing ones is ONE key-control duty seen from both ends, not two. The same holds for any procedure a worker conducts on one occasion and submits to on another: it is one competence, one plan, one duty. Do not split them.
  · A PURPOSE OR MEANS CLAUSE IS NOT A SECOND DUTY. A clause saying what the work is for, or by what means it is carried out, describes the same duty even though it contains another verb.
  · BUT TWO MEANS A READER WOULD COUNT SEPARATELY ARE TWO DUTIES, and this narrows the exemption just above. That exemption is for ALTERNATIVE means — interchangeable techniques for ONE instance of the work, where the worker picks one and the job is done. For a locksmith, "open a locked door by picking the cylinder or drilling it" is one duty: either way the door opens once. It is NOT for CUMULATIVE means, where BOTH happen, to the same recipient, each with its own preparation, its own occasion, or its own artifact. For a building surveyor, "report findings through a written schedule and a client walkthrough" is TWO duties: the schedule is drafted at a desk and the walkthrough is conducted on site, both are owed, and doing one does not discharge the other.
    THE TELL IS USUALLY "AND" RATHER THAN "OR". Alternatives are joined by "or" because one suffices; separate duties are joined by "and" because both are owed. Do not decide on the conjunction alone — ask whether one means substitutes for the other on a given occasion, or whether both are performed. If both are performed and each carries its own preparation, they are two duties however single the purpose they serve, and a statement naming both in a "through ..." or "by ..." clause is FUSED.
  · WHAT STILL COUNTS AS FUSED: parts that arise on SEPARATE OCCASIONS, from separate triggers, or as separate standing obligations the worker could be doing in any order and for unrelated reasons.     "develop", "implement", or "revise". "Recommend" terminates the worker's involvement at the proposal
    and is wrong wherever the work continues past it.
    TEST: ask who acts next. If the sentence ends at a proposal and SOMEONE ELSE would have to act for the
    work to be finished, "recommend" is right. If nobody else appears -- if the worker is the one who
    would carry it out -- the verb has stopped short of the deliverable. Say what they produce.
1.3 THE VERB MUST NOT CLAIM AN OUTCOME THE WORKER DOES NOT OWN. Verbs naming an organisational or
    political result — advance, secure, win, drive — attribute a multi-party outcome to one worker.
    Re-anchor the verb on the worker's own contribution and demote the outcome to the purpose clause.
1.4 PREFER THE LOWEST-ABSTRACTION VERB THAT IS STILL OCCUPATION-STANDARD. An umbrella verb is acceptable
    only if a practitioner at any employer would use the term unprompted. Otherwise decompose into the
    concrete action.
    THE USUAL OFFENDERS NAME NO ACT AT ALL: "manage", "handle", "conduct", "oversee", "deal with", "pursue",
    "ensure", and the synonyms of "do" — "perform", "execute", "use", "utilize". Each is a container for whatever follows it, which is why
    statements led by them always grow an enumeration behind — the vague head forces the tail to do the
    work. Replace the container with what the worker actually does; if no single concrete verb covers the
    activities, that is evidence of TWO tasks, not license for an umbrella.
1.4a LEAD WITH THE RESPONSIBILITY, NOT ITS FIRST CHORE. Where a statement covers the several acts that
    upkeep one continuing responsibility — opening a new file, running a stocktake, supervising staff,
    keeping one set of books — the HEAD VERB names the responsibility, and the chores follow in AT MOST
    ONE subordinate participial clause carrying a noun list ("Open new tenancy files, preparing reference
    checks and inventory records..."), never as a flat list of coordinate verbs with the
    responsibility buried or absent, and never as stacked "-ing" clauses — 1.4b's one-clause cap holds
    for this form too.
    TEST: read the head verb and object alone. If they name a step ("send reference requests") rather
    than the thing the worker is answerable for ("open new tenancy files"), re-anchor the sentence on the
    responsibility.
1.4b GERUNDS ARE A LAST RESORT. A statement carries AT MOST ONE participial ("-ing") clause. Chores and
    steps beyond that are DROPPED — the members carry the detail, and a statement need not enumerate its
    chores — or written another way. DROP THE CHORES, KEEP THE TEXTURE: the trimmed statement keeps a short
    tail naming the object kinds, the counterpart, or two or three OCCASIONS the duty serves ("for X, Y, or
    Z", "such as A or B"). A statement stripped to a bare verb and object has been over-trimmed — the target
    register is a finite verb (or two), an object list, a findable counterpart, and an occasions tail: a genuine second step takes a finite verb ("Prepare X and
    monitor Y"), an enumeration becomes a "such as" NOUN list, an outcome goes in the purpose clause.
    Stacked gerunds are the enumeration defect wearing grammar — two or more "-ing" clauses in one
    statement is the same smell as a verb chain, whatever introduces them.
    ONE "by X-ing" MEANS CLAUSE IS ALLOWED. Where the method carries the act's judgement or skill,
    a statement may carry one "by"-clause naming it — the standard O*NET shape, and it counts as the one
    permitted participial, not a stack, even when it coordinates TWO gerunds ("by taking X and
    reviewing Y"). TWO GERUNDS IS THE CEILING: three or more in the clause is the enumeration defect
    wearing "by" — keep the one or two moves that carry the judgement; the members hold the rest. The clause names
    the means of the MAIN verb; a gerund that is its own errand is a second duty and stays out.
1.4c A STATEMENT IS ABOUT 15 WORDS. That length holds one verb, one object list with an example or two,
    and one clause — which is all one duty needs. A statement pushing past ~20 words is carrying a second
    duty, a redundant clause, or an enumeration that belongs in a "such as" list cut to two or three
    items. Trim to what a reviewer can take in at a glance; the members carry the detail.
1.4d THE VERB MUST NAME THE WORK, NOT THE MANDATE. "Represent", "serve", and "act for" name the
    RELATIONSHIP under which work happens, not the work: everything an agent does for the principal who
    engaged them is representation, so a represent-led sentence says only who the worker was for. Lead with the concrete
    act performed under the mandate and demote the mandate to the purpose clause: "Survey boundaries, stake
    corners, and file the plat TO ACT FOR owners in a dispute" names the work and keeps the
    relationship. EXCEPTION: where standing in the role is itself the act — entering an appearance,
    covering a hearing where presence is the duty, or carrying a matter through an engagement whose span
    is the task ("from data calls to negotiated findings") — the role verb stands.
1.5 THE VERB MUST NAME THE WORK, NOT THE FORUM IT HAPPENED IN. "Meet with", "discuss", "check in with",
    "attend" and "talk to" name an occasion, not an accomplishment — they tell a reader where the worker
    was, not what they did or what changed. Name the act the occasion exists to perform and let the
    setting go, or demote it to an occasion clause where it is what makes the task distinct. For a
    building surveyor, "meet with contractors about defects" names the meeting; "agree remedial work
    with contractors" names the duty.
    TEST: ask what is different afterwards. If the only answer is "the conversation happened", the verb
    has named the forum. A verb that survives names something checkable — a decision reached, an
    instruction given, information obtained, an approval granted.
    NOT THIS: a conversational duty is not banned. Where the talking IS the work, use the specific verb
    for it — "interview", "negotiate", "counsel" — not the generic container.

## 2. VOCABULARY

2.1 NO HOUSE JARGON. The test: would this term appear in a job posting from a different employer, using a
    different methodology, in a different sector? If not, replace it with the plain equivalent.
2.2 NO CLIPPED OR ABBREVIATED FORMS, AND NO BARE ACRONYMS. Write the full word, and write out what the
    initials stand for.
    TEST: a CLIPPING is one word with its end cut off -- restore the letters and you recover ordinary
    English ("admin" -> "administrative", "spec" -> "specification"). An ACRONYM is the initials of several
    words. Both are written out; they differ only in how.
    NO EXCEPTION AND NO PARENTHETICAL. Not "<expansion> (<acronym>)": the initials add length where length
    is scarcest and tell a reader who already knew them nothing. Where the expansion alone reads badly the
    term is house jargon under 2.1 and the fix is a plainer phrase, not a shorter one.
    THERE IS NO EXEMPTION FOR NAMES. A named method, standard, programme or statute whose initials stand
    for words is written out like any other. Nor for clipped names: "C-section" is "caesarean section". The
    only question is whether the short form stands for something longer.
    A CLIPPING INSIDE A COMPOUND IS STILL A CLIPPING, and the compound is where it hides, because it reads
    as the name of a thing rather than as a shortened word: "app store", "in-app purchase", "admin panel",
    "spec review", "config file". Restore the letters.
    NOT A DEFECT: a capital that stands for no word at all -- "X-ray", "type 2", a model number. There is
    nothing to expand.

2.3 TERMS MUST BE NATIVE TO THE OCCUPATION. A term borrowed from an adjacent field signals the statement
    was drafted from the wrong template. Replace it with the occupation's own term.
    TEST: take each noun in turn and ask whose vocabulary it belongs to. A noun naming another trade's
    subject matter -- its livestock, its castings, its permits, its tolerances -- is borrowed even when
    the surrounding sentence is impeccable, and even when this occupation sometimes encounters the thing.
    Name what THIS occupation tracks about it instead.
2.4 STATEMENTS MUST BE COMPLETE. No mid-word or mid-clause truncation. Every statement is a grammatical
    sentence ending in a period.
2.5 A TERM MET ONLY IN ONE SPECIALTY DOES NOT BELONG IN AN OCCUPATION-LEVEL STATEMENT, whatever slot it
    fills — object, artifact, counterpart, procedure, statute, system, or setting. The statement describes
    the occupation; a term only one practice area's practitioners would use of their own work narrows the
    statement to that subfield and silently excludes everyone else.
    TEST: ask which practitioners could use this term of their own work. If only those in one practice
    area, sector, or client base could, replace it with the covering term at the occupation's level.
    AN ENUMERATED LIST OF SPECIALTY TERMS IS THE SAME DEFECT IN PLURAL, and the commoner shape, because it
    looks like coverage: each item is one practice area's instance, and the list silently excludes every
    specialty not on it.
    THE FIX KEEPS THE SHARED CORE BY NAME AND COVERS THE REST WITH ONE OPEN TAIL. An item every
    practitioner recognises stays; the specialty items fold into one covering phrase ("and other property
    owners", "or other regulated filings"). Where no item on the list is shared-core, the covering term
    replaces the whole list. The covering term must still be concrete — a role, an artifact kind, a
    category a reader can point to — never a collective that names nobody (2.1 and 5.2 still apply).
    NOT THIS: a concrete example inside a shared-core list is not a specialty term. "Such as" examples
    every practitioner recognises make a statement better (3.1a); the test is whether the term is met only
    inside one subfield, not whether it is specific.

## 3. SCOPE — ONE TASK, ONE ACTIVITY

3.1 OBJECT LISTS MUST BE CO-HYPONYMS. Every item in an "A, B, or C" list must name a thing the SAME
    activity is applied to. If one item is produced by a genuinely different process, it belongs in its
    own statement.
    TEST: substitute each item into the head on its own and ask whether the worker is doing the same thing
    each time. Same activity on different instances is ONE list, however varied the items look and however
    differently each reaches its recipient. A different activity splits out.
    Do NOT additionally require the items to match on workflow and on counterpart: that three-way test
    fails almost every real list and is the main source of wrong splits.
3.1a A LIST OF NEAR-SYNONYMS IS ONE ITEM. Co-hyponymy is necessary, not sufficient. Where two or three items
    name the same thing at slightly different scope or duration, they cost length and carry no information,
    and the sentence starts to read like a form rather than like the work. Collapse them to the plainest one
    and spend the words on a concrete example instead: one example a practitioner would recognise says more
    than three abstract near-equivalents.
    TEST: read the list in order and ask what item 2 tells a reader that item 1 did not. If the only answer is
    that it can be bigger, longer-term, more formal or more detailed, it is the same item twice — keep one.
    NOT THIS: this does not license dropping a genuinely different object to shorten a list. The items being
    collapsed have to be the same thing described twice, not two things the same activity is applied to.
3.1b OBJECT LISTS JOIN WITH "OR", NOT "AND". THE STATEMENT DESCRIBES AN OCCUPATION, NOT A PERSON, and that
    settles the conjunction. The list was assembled from activities reported by SEVERAL different workers, so
    it names what different practitioners do — one member handles the first kind of work on that list, another
    the second, a third neither. "A, B, and C" asserts that whoever does this task does all three, every time it occurs, which is
    false of an occupation by construction. "A, B, or C" says the activity applies to any of them, which is
    what a task inventory means.
    IT ALSO STOPS THE LIST READING AS SEPARATE DUTIES. A conjunction is how two duties are written, so "and"
    invites the reader to count the items; "or" tells them these are alternatives within one duty.
    TEST: put "any of" in front of the list. If the sentence is still a true description of the occupation's
    work, the list is disjunctive and takes "or". At occupation level almost every object list is — including
    ones a single worker really does handle together on a single occasion, because the next worker does not.
    THIS IS ABOUT OBJECTS, NOT VERBS. Verbs joined by "and" are governed by 3.2, which permits them where they
    are successive steps of one process — "draft and file", "record and submit". Do not change those.
    NOT THIS: the only objects that keep "and" are ones that are not alternatives at all — inseparable parts of
    a single artifact or act, where naming one without the others describes nothing anyone does.

3.2 VERB LISTS MUST NOT CONJOIN DISTINCT ACTIVITIES, AND SUCCESSIVE STEPS OF ONE PROCESS ARE NOT DISTINCT.
    Two shapes are acceptable. "Verb1 ... or Verb2 ..." where the verbs are ALTERNATIVE realisations of one
    activity, either of which finishes the job. And "Verb1 and Verb2 ..." where they are SUCCESSIVE STEPS of
    one process over the SAME object, ON ONE OCCASION — drafting a document and then checking it before it goes
    out, deciding an outcome and then telling whoever needs to know, fitting a part and then testing that it
    works. A worker who did the first and not the second has left one job half done, and a statement naming both
    describes that job completely rather than fusing two. Otherwise split the statement, or raise it to a
    genuine superordinate verb.
    NOT SUCCESSIVE, THOUGH IT SOUNDS IT: setting a rule and later applying it, making a plan and later working
    to it, producing a thing and later maintaining it. Each pair is one act done once and another done
    repeatedly afterwards, on occasions of its own — the second is not the finish of the first, it is the job
    the first made possible. Those split.
    BUT THE CHORES OF ONE ONGOING RESPONSIBILITY STAY TOGETHER, and this bounds the paragraph above: where
    the acts are the upkeep of one thing the worker is answerable for — recording entries and chasing the
    unresolved ones, directing daily work and periodically appraising it — no one of them is a duty on its
    own, and naming two or three of them describes the responsibility completely rather than fusing tasks.
    SUPERVISING ONE'S OWN STAFF IS THE COMMONEST SUCH RESPONSIBILITY, and its chores span both directions
    and all consequences: assigning and directing their work, answering their questions, unblocking their
    tasks, appraising their performance and settling what follows from the appraisal. A statement naming
    several of these is one supervisory duty described completely — question-and-answer inside the
    worker's own operation is not an exchange of sides, and an appraisal's consequences are not a second
    act.
    The produce-then-maintain split is for deliverables that leave the worker's own bookkeeping and are
    used by others.
    TEST: ask whether the second verb would ever be performed by someone who had NOT done the first, on a
    different occasion and for its own reason. If yes, they are separate duties and they split. If the second
    exists only because the first was done, they are one duty and they stay.
    NOT THIS: doing the work and WRITING ITS RESULT INTO A RECORD are not steps of one process. The recording
    is nearly always already a task of its own, so a statement naming both annexes that task's act — which is
    how one line comes to read as a duplicate of another.
3.3 REACTIVE AND GENERATIVE WORK ARE SEPARATE TASKS. Handling reported problems is a different activity
    from eliciting new requirements, even when both occur in the same conversation with the same
    counterpart.
3.4 OBJECT LISTS MUST BE DRAWN FROM THE OCCUPATION'S SHARED CORE, NOT ONE SPECIALTY. Where an occupation
    spans practice areas, specialty-specific objects narrow the statement to a subfield; generalise the
    list to the category that covers all of them.

## 4. PURPOSE, OCCASION AND METHOD CLAUSES

4.1 A PURPOSE CLAUSE MUST BE INFORMATIVE. Drop it where the verb already entails it.
    THE EASIEST CASE TO MISS IS THE MORPHOLOGICAL ONE: the clause is built on a word already standing in the
    head, so it restates it without repeating it. For a building surveyor, "measure floor areas to take
    measurements" and "schedule inspection visits to arrange scheduling" both say one thing twice, and neither
    reads as a restatement until you line the words up. CHECK THE STEMS, not the sense: if a noun or verb in
    your clause shares a root with a word in the head, the clause is the head with "to" in front. Say what the
    work FEEDS or DECIDES, or drop it.
    TEST: delete the clause and read the sentence again. If nothing was lost -- if a reader could have
    predicted the clause from the verb and object alone -- it was empty and it goes. Clauses naming what
    happens to anything sent anywhere ("for review", "for approval", "for their records") almost always
    fail this: submissions are reviewed by definition. Keep the clause only where it names the decision or
    outcome at stake, which a reader could not have guessed.
4.2 A PURPOSE CLAUSE MUST BE TRUE OF EVERY ITEM IN THE OBJECT LIST. If it holds for only part of the
    list, either drop the clause or split the statement.
4.2a AN OCCASION CLAUSE MUST NARROW WHEN THE WORK HAPPENS. "as needed", "when required", "in the course of
    the work", "on an ongoing basis", "during or after the working day" — these name no occasion at all. They
    are true of every moment the task could occur, so they add length and tell a reader nothing about when to
    expect the work.
    TEST: name an occasion the clause EXCLUDES. "before each shift" excludes mid-shift; "after an inspection
    finding" excludes the routine case; "at intake" excludes everything later. If you cannot name a time the
    clause rules out, delete it — the sentence is stronger without it.
    KEEP THE CLAUSE where the occasion is what makes this task different from a neighbouring one: the same act
    performed at a different trigger can be a different duty, and then the trigger is load-bearing and belongs
    in the sentence.

4.3 A METHOD CLAUSE MUST INFORM, AND AN INFORMATIVE ONE IS WELCOME. A "by ..." or "through ..." tail
    naming HOW the act is performed — the one or two moves that carry its judgement or skill ("by
    reviewing records and examining the patient") — is the standard O*NET shape for method
    and is LEGITIMATE even where the head alone already names the work: the method is the texture a reviewer
    wants. The clause is a DEFECT in exactly two cases: it REPEATS the head's stems ("measure areas by
    taking measurements" — check the roots, as 4.1 does), or it SMUGGLES A SECOND DUTY — a means item
    that is not a constituent move of the MAIN act but its own errand with its own occasion.
    IF THE HEAD GOES EMPTY without the clause — the "by ..." was carrying the only real content — the
    head was a category and the clause's contents are the actual tasks: promote one of them to the verb.
    NOT THIS, AND THE EXCEPTION IS NARROWER THAN IT SOUNDS. Naming a shared end and putting the activities
    after "through" is the repair for ONE defect: a statement whose activities need DIFFERENT VERBS and would
    read as two or three separate tasks if written as coordinate verb phrases. It does NOT apply to one verb
    over several objects — "prepare A, B, and C for X" is a plain object list and stays one.
    TEST THE EXCEPTION BEFORE CLAIMING IT: ask whether a single verb covers every activity. If one does, there
    was no defect to repair, and the "through" clause has traded a clean list for a category — which is the
    defect this principle exists to catch, arrived at from the other side. Never use the shape for a manner or
    a step.
    AND THE EXCEPTION IS NEVER A GERUND CHAIN. "by A-ing, B-ing, and C-ing" strings three activities behind
    the head the way a conjunction strings duties in front of it — the shape hides an enumeration, it does
    not repair one. Where the exception genuinely applies, name at most TWO activities after "through", or
    use the participial responsibility form of 1.4a; three or more "-ing" clauses after "by" or "through"
    is the defect itself, whatever the head says.

4.4 A STATE IS A GOAL, NOT A TASK. Some statements put a lasting condition where the object belongs — a
    disposition of people toward the worker or each other, a climate, a standing — something no single act
    produces, that persists between acts, and that no one could be watched doing. Work acts on an object a
    reader can see acted on; a condition like that is what the work is FOR. A statement whose object is such
    a condition has promoted its goal into the object slot and dropped the work: for a hotel concierge,
    "Build rapport with returning guests" names nothing a reader could watch. Write the observable act as
    the verb and object, and the condition as the purpose clause: "Greet returning guests by name and check
    in during their stay to build rapport." The activities name the acts; take the one or two that carry
    the duty.
    TEST: ask what the worker was seen DOING. If the sentence names no observable act, the work is missing
    and a goal is standing in its place.

## 5. COUNTERPARTS

5.1 INHERENTLY COORDINATIVE TASKS NAME THE COUNTERPART. Use published occupation titles where the
    counterpart is a specific occupation, and add "and other staff" to keep the statement open.
5.2 A GENERIC COLLECTIVE IS NOT A COUNTERPART. "stakeholders", "other parties", "personnel", "relevant teams",
    "decision-makers", "the business" — these name nobody. They tell a reader that somebody was involved without
    saying who, and they are to a counterpart what a bare category is to an object list: the reach without the
    evidence. Name the role, the function or the occupation; where the activities genuinely span several, name
    the two or three that recur and add "and other staff" to keep it open.
    A GENERIC WORD IS FINE AS THE OPEN TAIL, NEVER AS THE WHOLE COUNTERPART. 5.1 asks for that tail on purpose,
    so "the site foreman and other trades" is right while "other trades" alone is not — exactly as a category may
    head an object list but not replace it. Before flagging, check whether at least ONE named party appears
    beside the generic one. If one does, the sentence has its counterpart and the tail is doing its job.
    TEST: could a reader go and find the person? For a building firm, "the site foreman" and "the parts
    supplier" are findable; "stakeholders" is not. If the word survives being swapped for any other group in
    any other trade, it is naming nobody.
    THIS ONE IS WORTH ITS OWN LINE because a reviewer rejects it on sight: it reads as a statement written
    without asking who the work was for, and one such word can sink an otherwise sound sentence.
5.3 A COUNTERPART MUST BE SHARED-CORE, NOT SPECIALTY. This is 2.5 applied to the counterpart slot: a
    counterpart met only in one specialty's cases narrows the statement to that subfield the same way a
    specialty object does (3.4). Keep the counterpart every practitioner meets by name and fold specialty
    counterparts into the open tail (5.1); where none is shared-core, the covering role replaces the list.
    For a veterinarian, "negotiate treatment plans with dairy herd owners, racehorse trainers, or kennel
    operators" is three specialties, not the occupation — "with animal owners" covers them and everyone
    unlisted. The tail must still ride on a findable named party, never a collective (5.2).


## NAME THE RULE YOU ARE APPLYING

Every objection belongs to exactly one numbered section above, and `principle` is that section's name:

  verb         §1 VERB SELECTION — the verb claims an authority the occupation does not hold or
               understates one it does, names the forum instead of the work, or sits above the
               activities' own verb when a sharper one is available. ALSO §1.4-1.4d: a container verb
               from the offender list ("manage", "handle", "conduct", "oversee", "deal with", "pursue", "ensure",
               "perform", "execute", "use", "utilize");
               TWO OR MORE "-ing" clauses stacked in one statement (§1.4b — count them: a second
               participial clause is the defect, whatever introduces it; ONE "by X-ing" MEANS clause
               naming how the main verb's act is performed is allowed and NOT a defect, including up to
               TWO coordinated gerunds inside it; THREE OR MORE gerunds in the clause is the
               enumeration defect and IS flagged); a statement running well past
               ~20 words (§1.4c); or a mandate verb ("represent", "serve", "act for") leading where a
               concrete act should, outside §1.4d's exceptions.
               BE ESPECIALLY WARY OF THE CHORE-ENUMERATION SHAPE: a responsibility head trailed by a
               procedural inventory of its own chores — "including X-ing records, Y-ing responses, and
               Z-ing with counterparts", or the same list dressed as nouns. Walking the reader through
               the steps is the enumeration defect whatever the grammar; the members carry that detail,
               and §1.4b says the chores are DROPPED first. A statement that cannot say what the worker
               is answerable for without listing how they go about it draws this objection.
  vocabulary   §2 VOCABULARY — house jargon, a clipped or abbreviated form, a term borrowed from an
               adjacent field, a truncated statement.
  fusion       §3.2 / §3.3 — the statement conjoins ACTIVITIES that are separate duties, or fuses reactive
               with generative work. Two or more verbs, each with its own outcome.
  objects      §3.1 / §3.1a / §3.1b / §3.4 — the OBJECT LIST is malformed: items that are not co-hyponyms,
               two items that are near-synonyms of each other, "and" where alternatives want "or", or a
               list drawn from ONE SPECIALTY where the occupation spans several (§3.4 — generalise to the
               category that covers all of them).
               §3.4 HAS A TEST YOU CAN RUN ON THE ACTIVITY LIST YOU WERE GIVEN. Take each item in the
               statement's object list and find the activities that name it. If an item is named by ONE
               activity while the rest of the list is named by several, that item is one worker's specialty
               promoted into the statement, and the task has been narrowed to their subfield — say `objects`
               and quote it. The category that covers what all the activities name is what belongs there.
               A WELL-FORMED OBJECT LIST IS NOT A DEFECT AND IS NOT `fusion`. "unit, integration, and
               automated tests", "charts, notes, and clinical documentation", "toileting, incontinence care,
               and bathing" are one action over co-hyponyms, which §3.1 asks for. Naming several things the
               SAME act applies to is the statement being specific, and specificity is wanted. Flag the list
               only when you can say WHICH of the four rules above it breaks and quote the offending item.
  clauses      §4 PURPOSE, OCCASION AND METHOD CLAUSES — an uninformative purpose clause, a purpose that
               is untrue of part of the object list, an occasion clause that narrows nothing, or a
               "by ..." / "through ..." tail that repeats the head's stems or smuggles a second duty.
               A "by X-ing" clause enumerating the MEANS of the main act (§4.3) is legitimate and NOT
               a defect, even where the head alone names the work.
               ALSO §4.4, WHICH RUNS THE OTHER WAY: a lasting CONDITION standing in the OBJECT slot — a
               disposition of people toward the worker or each other, a climate, a standing; something
               that persists between acts and that no one could be watched doing — with no observable
               act anywhere in the sentence. The goal has been promoted into the object and the work
               dropped; the activity list you were given names the acts the statement should lead with.
               Say `clauses` and quote the abstraction.
  counterpart  §5 COUNTERPARTS — a coordinative task that does not name who it is done with, or names a
               generic collective ("stakeholders", "other parties", "relevant teams") instead of a
               counterpart.
  acronym      AN INITIALISM OR ACRONYM LEFT UNEXPANDED. Say `acronym` and quote the letters. A term whose
               expansion IS the jargon is still `acronym`: write the words and let §2 judge them.
               THE TEST IS STRUCTURAL. Take every run of capitals in the sentence and ask one question of
               each: do these letters stand for words? If they do it is an initialism and it is a defect --
               whatever the letters are, however short, and whether or not you recognise the thing they
               name. Ask it of each token you find rather than looking for terms you have seen before.
               BREVITY AND FAMILIARITY ARE NOT EXEMPTIONS. A two-letter form reads as an ordinary word
               rather than as initials; a form ubiquitous in the field stops looking like initials at all;
               a form naming a well-known method or statute looks like a name. Each is still letters
               standing for words. Slow down on the short ones.
               DOMAIN VOCABULARY THAT IS NOT AN INITIALISM IS NOT THIS. "Hoyer lift", "Medicaid",
               "gait belt" are words a practitioner says; they are not abbreviations and are not a defect.
  face_valid   WOULD A PRACTITIONER RECOGNISE THIS AS HOW THE WORK IS DESCRIBED? The statement is true,
               correctly scoped, and still reads as something no one in the occupation would say — an
               assembled O*NET-ese construction, a noun-heavy paraphrase of a plain act, or a framing
               borrowed from the list's own template rather than from the work. This is the one axis that
               is about RECOGNITION rather than a rule, so it carries a higher bar: only say `face_valid`
               when you can name what a practitioner would say instead. Do NOT use it as a home for
               awkwardness you cannot otherwise place — that is what the paragraph below forbids.

Pick the section the defect actually offends. Do NOT reach for a label because the sentence merely reads
awkwardly — awkwardness is not a section, and if no section is offended there is no defect. `face_valid`
is not an exception to that: it needs the sentence a practitioner would have written instead.

## FIRM OBJECTIONS VERSUS QUESTIONS

Objections come in two strengths.

Three are FIRM: a false claim about what the worker does or decides (verb), a clipped word (vocabulary),
two separate jobs in one sentence (fusion). The analyst states these flatly and asks for the fix. Predict
a defect on these whenever you can quote the words.

AND THE AUTHORITY CLAIM IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN MISSED, so test it explicitly on every statement rather
than waiting for it to look wrong. Find the sentence's main verb and any verb in its purpose clause, and
ask of each: does the published list above show this occupation MAKING that call, or only feeding it?
A verb that settles something — determine, approve, authorise, set, decide, evaluate-in-order-to-decide —
when the list shows the occupation advising, preparing, or recommending, is a false claim, and the softer
verb is wanted. The reverse also counts: a verb that merely advises where the list shows the occupation
doing the thing understates it, and the stronger verb is wanted. Both are defects of the VERB. Name the
verb to change; do not conclude anything about who owns the task.

House vocabulary (vocabulary) is a QUESTION rather than a firm objection: the analyst is asking whether a
term is in general use or can be simplified, not asserting that it is wrong. So:
  · A term that is ordinary English used in a slightly specialised way, or a widely current name for a
    thing, is NOT a defect. An analyst recognises those and passes them.
  · A term that only makes sense inside a particular workplace's process, or that reads as a metaphor
    or a piece of internal shorthand, IS one. It is the kind of word a reader would have to be told.
  When you are unsure which of those two a term is, say there is no defect.

## CALIBRATION

A defect is the exception, not the rule. It needs a trigger you can quote. Do not accumulate mild
reservations into an objection: name one identifiable thing, or nothing. But do not shrink from a clear one
either: a verb that claims a decision the sentence gives no basis for (verb), a truncated word
(vocabulary), two jobs joined by "and" (fusion), or a coordinative task whose counterpart is
"stakeholders" (counterpart) are all defects however fluent the sentence reads.

whether others also do it.
